spec.description: Where people observe wildlife in Ecuador and the Galápagos, and what they find: research-grade iNaturalist observations read live from the ArcGIS Living Atlas, as H3 cells over the whole record and the most recent observations as dots, with taxonomic, yearly and seasonal breakdowns and the most observed species.

options.content:
## Observed biodiversity in Ecuador

**More than 770,000 research-grade observations** uploaded to
[iNaturalist](https://www.inaturalist.org/) by over 21,000 people, covering
some 24,000 species of mainland Ecuador and the Galápagos. They are read live from the
*Feature Service* [iNaturalist Species Observations](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=996576ae63d4499c924aabea1c3d3768)
in the ArcGIS Living Atlas: **no download and no ETL**, every panel is a query
against the service.

Three things to know so as to read the map properly:

- **The dots are a sample; the hexagons are the total.** The service cuts off at
  10,000 features per request and nothing here pages, so the dot layer is the N
  most recent observations. The H3 cells come already aggregated by the service
  itself and cover them all. The figure to trust is the one in the
  **Observation effort** panel.
- **The hexagons carry no date.** They are historical totals: they follow neither
  "From year" nor the map's time brush. Everything else does.
- **This measures observation effort, not abundance.** iNaturalist records where
  people go and what they photograph. Quito and the Galápagos stand out for their
  observers as much as for their biodiversity.

To narrow things to a particular area, draw it on the map: the side panels and the
tables obey it.

options.content:
**Source** · [iNaturalist Species Observations](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=996576ae63d4499c924aabea1c3d3768),
ArcGIS Living Atlas of the World (Esri), a public service needing no credentials.
Original data from [iNaturalist](https://www.inaturalist.org/), a joint initiative
of the California Academy of Sciences and the National Geographic Society;
each observation keeps the licence whoever uploaded it chose.
The service publishes only *research-grade* observations (`quality_grade =
'research'`: dated, georeferenced, with a photo or sound, and of wild organisms)
and runs roughly **a month behind** the present.
**Extent** · a rectangle (`-92.0 −5.1 → −75.0 1.7`), not the country's border:
it drags in strips of Colombia, Peru and ocean. Real clipping is what the polygon
drawn on the map does.
